title: Start With Choice Before Strategy
reader_question: What does a player want before anyone else enters the story?
plain_language_goal: Learn why preferences, utility, and expected utility are the measuring tools underneath every later payoff table.
checkpoint: You should be able to explain why a payoff number is not raw happiness and why uncertainty requires weighting possible outcomes before choosing.

title: Represent The Strategic Situation
reader_question: What object keeps everyone's choices, timing, and payoffs visible?
plain_language_goal: Move from one-person choice to game representation: tables for simultaneous dependence, trees for time and information.
checkpoint: You should be able to say why judging one action alone is usually wrong, and when an action can be removed before equilibrium is solved.

title: Make Predictions Survive Deviations
reader_question: Can each player look at the proposed outcome and still want to stay put?
plain_language_goal: Understand equilibrium as a mutual consistency test, then see why conflict and randomization require sharper versions of the same idea.
checkpoint: You should be able to distinguish a stable prediction from a good social outcome, and explain why randomization can be strategic rather than confused.

title: Test Time, Threats, And Patience
reader_question: Will a promised future action still make sense when the future arrives?
plain_language_goal: Use backward reasoning, subgame checks, bargaining logic, and repeated-game discipline to separate credible plans from empty announcements.
checkpoint: You should be able to explain why a known last round can unravel cooperation, and why an indefinite future can sometimes discipline today's temptation.

title: Reason With Hidden Information
reader_question: What changes when players know different values, costs, types, histories, or facts that other players cannot directly see?
plain_language_goal: Track types, beliefs, updating, signaling, cheap talk, and common knowledge without treating beliefs as arbitrary story glue.
checkpoint: You should be able to explain why the same visible action can mean different things depending on type, cost, belief updating, and publicness.

title: Read Rules As Incentive Machines
reader_question: How do auction and market rules change what strategic people choose?
plain_language_goal: See mechanism and auction topics as design problems: the rule must make the desired behavior privately sensible.
checkpoint: You should be able to ask, for any rule, what a participant can gain by shading, hiding, misreporting, entering, or leaving.
